# Daniel 8: Research notes, verse by verse

Each point gives its source URL. I used only pages I actually read. Verses or topics I couldn't find are listed at the end.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading

**v. 1:** The vision came about two years after the one in chapter 7. Belshazzar may have been co-regent with his father Nabonidus, and we don't know for how long. From this chapter onward the book switches back from Aramaic to Hebrew. (https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-8) Constable dates "the third year" to about 551 BC and thinks this was a vision rather than a dream, probably in the daytime. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Guzik notes that Babylon was still firmly in power and Greece hardly mattered yet. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)

**v. 2:** Commentators disagree about whether Daniel was really in Susa. Guzik says he was there on the king's business (citing v. 27). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) Constable thinks Daniel was in Babylon and saw himself in Susa only in the vision. Susa later became a Persian capital, Esther's home, and the city Nehemiah left from. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Utley leaves the question open and lists other biblical visions where the prophet was carried somewhere (Ezekiel, Philip, John). He also says the old Greek, Aramaic and Latin versions read the "canal" as an "Ulai gate." (https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-8)

**v. 3:** The ram is Medo-Persia (v. 20). The taller horn that came up later is Persia, which became the stronger partner after the Medes. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) Guzik and Constable both say the ram was a Persian national emblem: Persian kings carried a ram's head into battle. Constable adds that in ancient astrology Aries stood for Persia and Capricorn for Greece. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary links the ram to the bear of 7:5. The ram here corresponds to the bear of Daniel 7:5, symbolizing clumsy firmness (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/daniel-8.html)

**v. 4:** Persia pushed west, north and south but made no major conquests to the east. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) Utley reads the three directions alongside the three ribs in the bear's mouth (7:5). He hears arrogance in "did as he pleased and became great." He also warns that apocalyptic details are "fuzzy": Greece did in fact push Persia back in 490 and 480 BC. (https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-8) Constable quotes Goldingay: when this phrase about doing great things is used of humans, it tends to suggest arrogance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)

**v. 5:** The goat is Greece and the prominent horn is Alexander the Great. "Without touching the ground" pictures how fast he conquered. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-8:1-27) Matthew Henry gives two readings: the goat moved so lightly it seemed to fly, or none touched him in the earth, that is, he met with little or no opposition (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_008.cfm) Calvin says the goat was borne along with a rapid impulse, like that of lightning itself. (https://www.ccel.org/study/Dan_8:5-8:5) Guzik cites Clarke, who cites Newton, that Greeks were called "the goats' people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)

**vv. 6–7:** The goat's rage reflects Greek anger over earlier Persian invasions. Alexander's rapid conquest of the Persians involved three battles of major significance which he won against overwhelming odds: Granicus (334 B.C.), Isus (333 B.C.), and Gaugemela (331 B.C.). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_8_commentary) Utley notes that a reader of Daniel alone would expect one battle, not three: the prophecy is "true, but fuzzy." (https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-8)

**v. 8:** The large horn breaking is Alexander's sudden death at about 32. The four horns are Cassander (Greece), Lysimachus (Asia Minor), Seleucus (Syria and Israel's land) and Ptolemy (Egypt). Guzik adds that God used the spread of Greek to prepare the world for the Gospel, since koine Greek became the language of the New Testament. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) Constable says Alexander also grew arrogant, treating himself as divine. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) The Pulpit Commentary draws a moral: Alexander was to the kingdom of Macedon merely a horn—a weapon of offence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-8.html)

**v. 9:** The little horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Seleucid king. He gained the throne through murder, flattery and bribery. Jews twisted his title "Epiphanes" into "Epimanes," meaning "madman." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) Sam Storms says virtually everyone also acknowledges that the 'little horn of chp. 8 is Antiochus Epiphanes, Syrian ruler of the 2nd century b.c. who persecuted the Jews. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-8:1-27) Constable says the directions are measured from Syria and that "the Beautiful Land" is Palestine. He thinks this horn is clearly different from the little horn of chapter 7. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)

**v. 10:** Constable takes the "stars" to be Israel, recalling the promise of descendants as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5). He thinks "host" and "stars" probably mean the same thing. Some read the host as angels, but he argues v. 12 makes that unlikely. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Barnes says Antiochus east down and trampled on the princes, and rulers, and people, of the holy host or army of God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-10.html) Peake reads the attack on the stars as a symbol of Antiochus trying to destroy the Jewish religion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/daniel-8.html)

**v. 11:** Peake says the prince of the host: i.e. God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/daniel-8.html) Constable explains that the "daily sacrifice" (Hebrew *tamid*) was the regular morning and evening offering. Antiochus did not physically tear the temple down; he made it unusable for true worship. Some, like Walvoord, also see a future fulfillment (cf. 9:27). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Guzik retells the December 168 BC events from 1 Maccabees: an idol of Zeus set up and swine offered on the altar. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)

**v. 12:** There are two readings of "in the rebellion":
- God handed Israel over to Antiochus because of the Jews' own sin. Guzik takes this view and points to the high-priest bribery scandals of Jason and Menelaus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)
- Constable sets this view (Archer) beside Walvoord's, that the rebellion is Antiochus's own. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)

Gill says "casting truth to the ground" means Antiochus tried to extirpate and abolish true religion and godliness; he cut in pieces the copies of the book of the law, and burnt them (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-12.html)

**v. 13:** Constable takes the holy ones to be angels. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Guzik: Many think this nameless holy one is an Old Testament appearance of Jesus. This is possible, but there is not enough information to be certain. (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Dan/Dan_8.cfm) Storms connects the "rebellion that causes desolation" with the pig sacrificed on the altar to Zeus in December 167 BC. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-8:1-27)

**v. 14:** The main literal readings are:
- **2,300 full days**, about six years and four months. Guzik prefers this, counting back from the temple's cleansing on December 25, 165 BC to 171 BC. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Dan/Dan-8.cfm)
- **1,150 days**, counting 2,300 morning and evening sacrifices. Constable lists who holds which view and prefers 2,300 days. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)
- **A symbolic number** close to three and a half years. Utley/bible.org favours this, linking it to 7:25. (https://bible.org/seriespage/daniel-8)

The Pulpit Commentary ties the period to the time between Antiochus's desecration and Judas Maccabaeus's cleansing. (https://biblehub.com/daniel/8-14.htm) Constable notes the cleansing is remembered at Hanukkah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)

**vv. 15–16:** Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says The eternal Son of God stood before the prophet in the appearance of a man, and directed the angel Gabriel to explain the vision. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/8-17.htm) Coffman notes this is the first time the Bible names a holy angel. It is the same Gabriel who later came to Zechariah and Mary. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-17.html) JFB says "Gabriel" means "the strength of God." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Dan/Dan_008.cfm)

**v. 17:** Keil says "son of man" reminds Daniel he is only human. "Time of the end" is the prophet's term for the end of his prophetic horizon, which here is Antiochus's time. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/daniel-8.html) Benson gives two readings: a fixed time of fulfillment, or a fulfillment nearly 400 years away. He says Daniel fell down because he couldn't bear the angel's brightness, not to worship him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/8-17.htm) Ellicott cites Jerome: what happened under Antiochus was a pattern for what Antichrist will do. (https://biblehub.com/daniel/8-17.htm)

**vv. 18–19:** Keil takes "wrath" to mean the wrath of God against Israel, the punishment which God hung over them on account of their sins (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/8-20.htm) Matthew Henry says the vision will become clear once the events happen, and the events will become clear through the vision. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_008.cfm)

**vv. 20–22:** Constable says the ram is Media and Persia together, not Media alone. The goat is Greece, not Persia. He presents these as answers to the critical view (see Part 3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html) Matthew Henry notes the four kingdoms never reached Alexander's stature. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_008.cfm)

**vv. 23–25:** The Biblical Illustrator applies "insolent king, skilled in intrigue" to Antiochus, noted for hard-hearted cruelty and crafty dissimulation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-12.html) Guzik says Antiochus fits every detail, including "broken off, but not by human hands": God brought him down by disease. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)

**v. 26:** Gill says the 2,300 should be understood literally, as ordinary days. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/daniel/8-26.html) Barnes suggests the name "evenings and mornings" may come from the evening and morning sacrifice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-26.html)

**v. 27:** Guzik uses this verse to show that Daniel was in Susa on the king's business (see v. 2). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/) I found no further comment on Daniel's illness.

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

**Antiochus only, or Antiochus and Antichrist (vv. 9–14, 17–25):**
- **Lutheran and Reformed:** Guzik quotes both reformers. Martin Luther wrote, "This chapter in Daniel refers both to Antiochus and Antichrist." John Calvin wrote, "Hence Luther, indulging his thoughts too freely, refers this passage to the masks of Antichrist." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Dan/Dan-8.cfm)
- **Pentecostal and charismatic (Guzik, Calvary Chapel):** The prophecy was fulfilled in Antiochus but also points to the future Antichrist, like a near and a far focus. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)
- **Dispensational (Constable, quoting Archer):** Antiochus is a prototype of the end-time little horn of chapter 7, and Jesus pointed this way in Matthew 24:15. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)
- **Sam Storms:** It depends on how you read chapter 7. If Rome is the fourth kingdom, the two little horns are different people. If Greece is, both chapters describe Antiochus. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-8:1-27)

**2,300 days or 2,300 years (v. 14):**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Natural days only. Those who receive it of years and months are wretchedly mistaken, and even ridiculous in their calculations. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-14.html)
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** Clarke takes the opposite view: I think the prophetic day should be understood here, as in other parts of this prophet, and must signify so many years. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-14.html) On v. 26 he says the vision covers Not less than two thousand three hundred years! (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/8-26.html)
- **Baptist (John Gill):** Literal days fulfilled under Antiochus. Because Antiochus foreshadows Antichrist, though, the days may be considered as so many years, which will bring it down to the end of the sixth Millennium (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/8-14.htm)

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Seventh-day Adventist (v. 14):** Ellen White taught that the close of the 2300 days, in 1844—began the work of investigation and blotting out of sins. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/white/controversy.xxxi.html) Storms tells how William Miller predicted Christ's return for 1843–44, and how a follower then moved the date to the autumn of 1844. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/daniel-8:1-27) Guzik calls this year-day reading "tragic." He says the prophecy was already fulfilled before Jesus, who attended the Feast of Dedication. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Dan/Dan-8.cfm) Constable says the link to evenings and mornings probably limits the number to days. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)

**Modern critical scholarship (date of Daniel):** I didn't reach the critics' own pages, so this view comes only through its opponents:
- Constable says many "liberal" interpreters read the ram as Media alone and the goat as Persia because they date Daniel to the 2nd century BC. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-8.html)
- Guzik says Antiochus fits so well that critics insist Daniel was written after his time. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-8/)
- The Pulpit Commentary argues back: a writer in Maccabean times would have shown Alexander as a ram, because coins showed him with ram's horns. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-8.html)
- A Bible Hub article cites a Qumran scroll of Daniel 8 (about 125 BC) as evidence against the late date. (https://biblehub.com/q/Daniel_8_11_and_temple_desecration_link.htm)

**Catholic and Orthodox:** I only found Jerome, quoted second-hand by Ellicott. Jerome held that Antiochus was a pattern of Antichrist. (https://biblehub.com/daniel/8-17.htm)

---

**Not found:** I ran out of searches before reaching netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are missing. I also found nothing specific on v. 24's "not by his own power" and little on v. 27.
